newsitem.title: USA: Dlr opens higher in U.S., spotlight on FOMC confab.
newsitem.headline: Dlr opens higher in U.S., spotlight on FOMC confab.

text.p: The dollar started the week stronger against the mark and yen as some traders closed out short positions before a meeting of the policy-setting Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) on Tuesday, dealers said.
Dollar gains followed an overnight slump to 114.85 yen after news that Japan's trade surplus more than doubled in April from a year earlier to 831.48 billion yen.
Ben Strauss, an assistant vice president at Bank Julius Baer and Co, attributed dollar strength to a little short covering ahead of the FOMC tommorrow.
Still Strauss warned the market is probably not "respectful enough" of a potential rate increase on Tuesday.
"I don't think the market is long nearly enough dollars to account for the sizable potential for a hike," he added.
The greenbacked fetched 1.7032/37 marks at the open, up from 1.6920/30 marks at Friday's close. Against the yen, the dollar climbed to 116.25/30 from 115.65/75.
Dealers noted the dollar had triggered stop loss buy orders above 1.70 marks. A test of 1.7050 marks is possible, with the next significant resistance pegged in the area of 1.7090 marks to 1.7120.
Dealers also sketched near term resistance for dollar/yen at 116.40, and cited talk that trust banks have interest to sell dollars on any move up to 116.80 yen.
They were also careful to note that dollar gains came in thin volume on Monday.
"Europe is out. So, the market is very quiet," said Thomas Arnold, a vice president and chief dealer at Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank.
Financial markets in most of Europe were closed for the Whit Monday holiday.

In addition to the huge increase in the Japan's overall custom cleared trade surplus, the politically sensitive trade surplus with the United States ballooned 174.1 percent in April from a year earlier to 468.97 billion yen.

Japanese government spokesman Seiroku Kajiyama on Monday told reporters the rise in the overall surplus was due to the weakness of the yen. The dollar had soared to 127.45 yen on May 1, its highest level in 56 months.
"It serves their purpose to admit what it's about because they don't want the yen any weaker," said Kevin Harris, an international economist at MCM CurrencyWatch.
Harris pointed out that a lot of Japanese exporters are located off shore now.
"A weaker yen simply means that their exporters can't sell as much to their home market as they like," Harris said.
He also noted that Japan imports a lot of raw materials and imported goods become very expensive when the yen is weak.

While no key U.S. economic data were scheduled for release on Monday, U.S. international trade figures are due out Wednesday at 0830 EDT/1230 GMT. Economists polled by Reuters predicted, on average, the trade gap shrank to $10.3 billion in March from $10.42 billion in February.

As for the possibility of a Fed rate increase on Tuesday, Harris said, if the central bank does hike rates, there will likely be a fairly lengthy hiatus before the FOMC will have to think about tightening again.

Fed policymakers had increased the federal funds rate by 25 basis points to 5.50 percent on March 25, the first tightening in more than two years. After the Tuesday confab, the next FOMC meeting will be in early July.
In other trade, the dollar opened at 1.4225/35 Swiss francs, up from 1.4195/05 francs at Friday's close.
Sterling climbed to $1.6385/90 from $1.6360/70.
Shortly after the open, the dollar traded around Canadian $1.3727/32, littled changed from C$1.3730/35 at the previous close.
The Australian dollar opened at $0.7725/30, down from $0.7760/65.
